newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine labour to Peronists: Change or lose vote.
newsitem.headline: Argentine labour to Peronists: Change or lose vote.

text.p: Argentina's top union leader predicted on Monday the ruling party would lose legislative elections next year unless it scrapped austerity measures and plans to loosen labour laws.
Rodolfo Daer, general secretary of the Confederacion General del Trabajo (CGT), told Reuters he perceived little will in President Carlos Menem's Peronist government to ease free market reforms.

"If things don't change, social conflict will exist and deepen," he said in an interview. "People use their vote to reward or punish. If things continue as they are, the ruling party will not have a favourable electoral result next year."

The CGT was long the backbone of Peronists, who hold a majority in Congress. But it has clashed with Menem this year over worker benefit cuts, tax hikes and plans to reform labour laws and end the unions' virtual monopoly on health care.
The CGT, whose unions represent nine million workers, about a quarter of Argentina's population, held a 24-hour general strike in August and a 36-hour stoppage in September.
With a picture on his wall of former President Juan Peron, whose movement brought Menem to power for two consecutive terms, Daer described a rare chill in relations between labour and government.
Menem has departed from Peron's populist style and his market policies have led to clashes with unionized workers, the party's traditional allies.
"Unfortunately, it is true that, as in few times in our history, the relations between the government and the labour movement are very distant," Daer said.

Menem says scrapping collective wage deals and swapping redundancy payouts for unemployment insurance are the best way to combat the high jobless rate, now at 17 percent against seven percent when he first took office in 1989.

Striving to bridge an expected $6 billion fiscal gap this year, Menem has threatened to push this policy through Congress by decree. Unions control many Peronist deputies, without whose support passage of the bills could be hard.
Daer said the right to collective bargaining "is one of the fundamental issues over which we will not step back."
Both the government and the CGT have indicated they are willing to hold talks to reach a truce, but Daer denied news reports that secret negotiations were under way.
He said the CGT would sit across the table with the government when clear signs emerged they could lead to a rollback in the government's plans.
"We have not perceived this yet," he said. "If this does not happen they would be pushing us toward a fight."
